intro: This guide takes your group through The Life of Trust (For Teens) in twelve weeks, one chapter a week. It tells the true story of George Müller, a young thief and liar who was turned around by God and went on to care for orphans in Bristol by asking no one but God for what they needed. It is written for teenagers aged about 13 to 18 and suits a youth group, a homeschool or a small group.

Each session takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Open by saying the memory verse together (3 minutes). Read the chapter, either aloud together or at home beforehand (5–10 minutes). Talk through the chapter’s three questions, which come with answers to help you (10 minutes). Do the activity (10 minutes). Then close by praying, in your own words or inviting a volunteer to pray, about what the chapter raised (2–3 minutes). Each chapter ends with a “One thing to do” challenge, which is worth reading out before people leave.

To prepare, read the chapter yourself and glance at the activity; most weeks need only paper and pens. The story touches some tender places: Müller’s mother dies while he is out playing cards, his father threatens to disown him, a young woman pays off the debts of a father who drank, and money is tight on almost every page. Some of your group may know family conflict, a parent’s drinking or real financial pressure at home, so speak gently, never ask anyone about their own family or money, and keep any giving challenge about time and effort as much as cash. Let personal reflection stay private, and be ready to talk one-to-one with anyone the story stirs up.

weeks.summary: As a boy George Müller stole from his father, once hiding the money in his shoe, and lying became a way of life; the night his mother was dying, he was out playing cards. At sixteen he was jailed for running out on an inn bill, and two hours after release he chose a troublemaker as his travelling companion. Outwardly he was a top student bound for university, but inside he was empty and every vow to change came to nothing. The big idea: you can be respected and rotten at the same time, but your track record is not the final word on you.

memory_verse.text: Whoever conceals his transgressions will not prosper, but he who confesses and forsakes them will obtain mercy.

activity.title: Reputation and Reality
steps: Draw a line down the middle of a sheet of paper and label the sides “What people saw” and “What was really going on.”
As a group, fill in both columns for George Müller using the chapter.
Discuss why good intentions and promises to change did nothing for him on their own.
Ask each person to write privately, for themselves only, one true thing they want to bring honestly to God this week.
Fold the papers and let everyone keep their own.

weeks.summary: In November 1825 a fellow student, Beta, mentioned a Saturday evening meeting where people read the Bible, sang and prayed, and George asked to come. The host told him, “Come as often as you please; house and heart are open to you,” and George saw a man kneel to pray for the first time. Even then he proudly thought he could pray better, yet he went home “peaceful and happy” and called that ordinary evening the turning point of his life. The big idea: a life with God can begin quietly, through an ordinary invitation and an open door.

memory_verse.text: And he arose and came to his father. But while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran and embraced him and kissed him.

activity.title: Undramatic Beginnings
steps: Read Müller’s words aloud: “I obtained joy without any deep sorrow of heart, and with scarcely any knowledge.”
Discuss: why do people sometimes think a faith story has to be dramatic to count?
In pairs, list what made that room welcoming to a proud, confused student.
As a group, turn the list into three practical ways your own group could make newcomers feel the door is open.
Agree on one of them to try in the coming weeks.

weeks.summary: Full of new faith, George wrote to his father and brother urging them to seek God and got an angry letter back. When he wanted to become a missionary, his father raged, said he would no longer count him a son, and then wept and begged, which George found “by far the harder trial.” George decided to take no more money from him, and soon American professors hired him as a tutor and paid him “enough and to spare.” The big idea: loving God first can cost us with people we love, and God can provide what obedience costs.

memory_verse.text: Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me.

activity.title: Deciding in Advance
steps: Point out that Müller had already counted the cost before the pressure came.
In small groups, write two or three made-up situations where doing right might disappoint a parent, coach or friend.
Swap situations with another group and talk through how to respond with both conviction and love.
Discuss: why is pressure that cries harder to resist than pressure that shouts?
Ask each person to note privately one area where they want to decide now what they will do.

weeks.summary: In 1830, as pastor of a small church in Teignmouth, Müller gave up his salary of fifty-five pounds a year. It came from pew-rents, which gave the best seats to those who paid, people sometimes gave grudgingly, and the money had briefly tempted him to keep quiet about his beliefs on baptism. From then on he would accept free gifts through a box in the chapel but never ask anyone for anything, and he found refusing to drop hints even harder than giving up the salary. The big idea: money and approval can quietly buy our silence, so we must know where our leash is.

memory_verse.text: And my God will supply every need of yours according to his riches in glory in Christ Jesus.

activity.title: Where Is the Leash?
activity.materials: A whiteboard or large sheet of paper
steps: List Müller’s three reasons for giving up the salary on the board.
Ask the group to name things that can quietly control what teenagers say or don’t say, such as friends, followers, grades or money.
For each, discuss how it might “buy silence” in everyday life.
Ask: what did Müller gain by being “poor and free” rather than “paid and muzzled”?
Invite everyone to think privately about which leash pulls on them most.

weeks.summary: On Sunday 27 November 1831 the Müllers had twopence-halfpenny and barely enough bread for the day, so George asked God plainly for bread for the evening. While he was still praying, a poor woman knocked, bringing some of her own dinner and five shillings, and later returned with a large loaf. The book warns that famous legends about Müller are bigger than what he recorded; God’s answers usually came through ordinary people who were moved to act, and Müller admits days when he was tempted to distrust. The big idea: we can ask God plainly for real needs and watch for the ordinary ways he answers.

memory_verse.text: Give us this day our daily bread.

activity.title: Legend or Ledger?
steps: Explain the chapter’s warning that stories about Müller often get exaggerated.
Read out the plain record of 27 November 1831 from the chapter.
In pairs, discuss why the real, smaller answer might be more encouraging than a dramatic legend.
Each person writes privately one real, specific need to pray about this week.
Encourage everyone to note how and when an answer comes, and bring it back if they wish.

weeks.summary: In Bristol Müller saw believers worn out and afraid about money, and he wanted to give them visible proof that God still answers prayer by caring for orphans without asking anyone for a penny. He tested his motives hard, praying for days and asking a friend to probe for pride, and he remembered an orphan boy sent away to a distant poorhouse. In December 1835 he took hold of the words “Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it,” asked for a building, a thousand pounds and helpers, and two days later received one shilling. The big idea: big faith and honest checking of our motives belong together.

memory_verse.text: I am the LORD your God, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. Open your mouth wide, and I will fill it.

activity.title: The Müller Test
steps: Ask everyone to write privately one thing they would ask God for if they really believed he could do it.
As a group, list honest questions Müller might ask to test whether a dream is about God and others or mostly about me.
Each person runs their own idea through the questions, privately.
Discuss: why do some people dream big without checking motives, while others never ask God for much at all?

weeks.summary: At the December 1835 meeting to explain the orphan house, Müller made sure there was “purposely no collection” and no emotional appeal, and only ten shillings was given, yet he went home full of confidence. Gifts then began arriving unasked: a wardrobe, dishes, cutlery, fabric and blankets, a brother and sister offering to run the house without salary, then fifty and a hundred pounds. On 21 April 1836 the first orphan house opened with seventeen children. The big idea: work done God’s way, without pressure or manipulation, depends on his Spirit and shows his hand.

memory_verse.text: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.

activity.title: Pitch Without Pressure
steps: In small groups, choose a good cause such as a food bank or a youth event.
Write a short, honest appeal for it with no exaggeration, no guilt-tripping and no emotional pressure.
Read the appeals aloud and let the group point out any spin that crept in.
Discuss why Müller chose the slower, riskier way and what it proved.

weeks.summary: A. L., a poor seamstress earning about three shillings and sixpence a week, inherited four hundred and eighty pounds. Though her father had died in debt from drinking and she owed his creditors nothing, she quietly paid them in full, gave her mother a hundred pounds and sent a hundred to the orphan house, saying, “The Lord Jesus has given his last drop of blood for me, and should I not give him this hundred pounds?” She kept living plainly, told almost no one, gave until it was all gone, and in her poverty God provided for her through another believer. The big idea: real generosity gives what we will feel, and gives it quietly to God.

memory_verse.text: Truly, I say to you, this poor widow has put in more than all those who are contributing to the offering box. For they all contributed out of their abundance, but she out of her poverty has put in everything she had, all she had to live on.

activity.title: Quiet Giving
steps: Read A. L.’s sentence about the Lord Jesus giving his last drop of blood.
As a group, brainstorm ways teenagers can give that cost something real: time, effort, a comfort, a skill.
Discuss why giving that no one sees is so much harder than giving everyone sees.
Each person chooses privately one thing to give this week and decides to tell no one.

weeks.summary: In autumn 1838, with around a hundred people to feed in three orphan houses, money came in “by the day now, and almost by the hour,” and some days nothing came. Müller and his coworkers refused to go into debt, and on one of the worst days he wrote out eleven reasons why God should send help. His coworkers gave their own money; one sold his watch and gold pins, and one woman gave her last sixteen shillings. The big idea: a slow answer is not the same as no answer, so we keep praying honestly without quitting or cheating.

memory_verse.text: Father of the fatherless and protector of widows is God in his holy habitation.

activity.title: Eleven Reasons
steps: Read out some of Müller’s reasons for asking God to send help.
Discuss: is it right to bring God arguments and reasons? What does it show about Müller’s faith?
Ask each person to choose privately a prayer they have nearly given up on.
Have them write down, for themselves only, the real and specific reasons they are asking.
Close the activity by naming together the next honest step that can be taken while waiting.

weeks.summary: On 18 September 1838, with funds gone, a woman finally brought three pounds, two shillings and sixpence that her daughter had sent; she had been lodging next door to the boys’ orphan house with the money for four or five days. Müller saw it as proof that help was in God’s heart from the beginning, and that God let them pray long because he delights in his children’s prayers. Weeks later a letter with ten pounds was laid on the table while the coworkers were still on their knees. The big idea: silence is not absence, and God’s help may be nearer than we think while we wait.

memory_verse.text: Before they call I will answer; while they are yet speaking I will hear.

activity.title: Tracing the Answer
steps: Ask each person to think of a time something they hoped or prayed for came late.
Have them draw a simple timeline privately, marking when they started waiting and when the answer came.
On the timeline, mark anything that was already moving before they saw it.
Invite anyone who wants to share a story with the group, without pressure.
Discuss Müller’s idea that waiting can be part of the gift.

weeks.summary: In February 1839 visitors to the boys’ orphan house asked the matron whether they had a good stock of funds, and she replied, “Our funds are deposited in a bank which cannot break,” though there was not a penny in hand that day. The visitor was moved to tears, and the gentleman gave five pounds as he left. Müller was careful and kept out of debt, but he would not let his heart rest on anything that could fail. The big idea: every earthly security can break, so our ultimate trust belongs in God, who cannot.

memory_verse.text: But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven, where neither moth nor rust destroys and where thieves do not break in and steal.

activity.title: Banks That Break
steps: As a group, list things people rely on to feel secure, such as savings, grades, popularity, looks or a plan B.
For each, discuss how it could fail.
Ask: why could the matron be calm with no money in the house?
Ask each person to write privately the one thing they most count on to feel safe.
Challenge them to trust God with one thing this week they would normally handle by holding on tight.

weeks.summary: Müller had weak health and slept in and napped to rest, but found his soul running on empty. In Plymouth in 1839 a friend said the best part of our time should be given to communion with the Lord, so Müller began rising early, with about seven hours’ sleep, to pray and read Scripture first, and his health improved. He did not make it a rigid rule, but asked who gets the best part of the day. The big idea: a life of trust is built by giving God the best of our time before anything else claims it.

memory_verse.text: And rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed.

activity.title: The First Ten Minutes
steps: Ask everyone to write down privately what they usually do in the first ten minutes after waking.
Discuss the chapter’s point that Müller’s enemy was a warm bed and ours is often a bright screen.
In pairs, plan a realistic first ten minutes with God: where the phone goes, what to read, how to pray.
Challenge everyone to try it for the next week.
Look back over the whole book together and name what most stood out about Müller’s life of trust.
